lesson.title: Mass Packed Into Space: Understanding Density
lesson.summary: Density relates a substance's mass to the volume it occupies, giving chemists a fixed, measurable property that identifies materials and explains why some substances float while others sink.
lesson.body:
Density is defined as the amount of mass packed into a given volume, expressed with the simple equation d = m / V, where mass is usually measured in grams and volume in either milliliters or cubic centimeters, two units that happen to be equal in size, so 1 mL = 1 cm^3. Density connects two ideas already introduced in Matter and Measurement: matter is anything with mass that occupies space, and density is precisely the ratio between those two properties for a given sample. Unlike mass or volume alone, density does not depend on how much of a substance you have. A gold ring and a gold bar have very different masses and volumes, but they share the same density, about 19.3 g/mL, because density is an intensive property, a characteristic of the substance itself rather than of any particular sample.

This makes density one of the most useful identifying properties in chemistry. If you measure the mass and volume of an unknown metal sample and calculate its density, you can compare that number against a table of known densities to make a strong guess about what the metal is, the same way a fingerprint identifies a person. Aluminum has a density near 2.70 g/mL, iron near 7.87 g/mL, and lead near 11.34 g/mL, values distinct enough that a simple mass and volume measurement can usually distinguish between them even without any chemical test.

Consider a worked example. A student is given an irregularly shaped piece of metal and measures its mass on a balance as 54.0 g. To find its volume, she drops it into a graduated cylinder containing 20.0 mL of water and watches the water level rise to 26.0 mL, a technique called water displacement that works because the solid pushes aside a volume of water exactly equal to its own volume. The metal's volume is therefore 26.0 mL minus 20.0 mL, or 6.0 mL. Dividing, d = 54.0 g / 6.0 mL = 9.0 g/mL. Comparing this to known densities, this value sits closest to copper, whose density is about 8.96 g/mL, so the student can reasonably conclude the sample is likely copper.

Density also explains everyday floating and sinking. Any object placed in a fluid will float if its density is less than the fluid's density, and sink if its density is greater. Ice floats on liquid water because ice, at about 0.92 g/mL, is actually less dense than liquid water at 1.00 g/mL, an unusual property caused by the open, hexagonal arrangement water molecules form when they freeze, which spaces the molecules farther apart than they are in the liquid. Most other substances become denser when they solidify, since freezing typically packs molecules closer together, which is exactly why water's behavior is considered an anomaly worth remembering.

Temperature also affects density, though it does not affect mass. As a substance is heated, its particles gain kinetic energy and spread slightly farther apart on average, increasing its volume while its mass stays fixed, which lowers its density. This is why hot air balloons rise: the heated air inside the balloon is less dense than the cooler air outside it, so the balloon experiences a net upward buoyant force. Because density depends on temperature, precise density values in reference tables are always reported at a specified temperature, commonly 25 degrees Celsius or 4 degrees Celsius for water, which is the temperature at which liquid water reaches its maximum density of 1.000 g/mL.
